title: Composition factors and affine linkage for dominant induced modules
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]: it is smooth, connected, affine and of finite type, has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, and every surjective homomorphism from a semisimple group with finite central kernel is an isomorphism. Solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial; finite central means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and commuting after every scalar extension. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq S$ and a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with unipotent radical $U$, with these notions as in [lem-sfb-rho-section-modules]. Use the character lattice $X=X^*(T)$, roots $\Phi$, positive roots $\Phi^+$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$, simple roots $\Delta$, coroots and integer pairing of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Put $\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha\in X$ as in [lem-sfb-rho-section-modules]. A rational $S$-module is an $F$-vector space $V$ with coaction $c_V:V\to V\otimes_F F[S]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity. A submodule is a linear subspace stable under this coaction, and simple means nonzero with only zero and itself as submodules. Write $V^U$ for the vectors whose restricted coaction is $v\mapsto v\otimes1$. A finite-dimensional simple module has highest weight $\eta\in X$ if $V^U$ is one-dimensional and $t v=\eta(t)v$ on this line after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. Write $\dim_F$ for ordinary vector-space dimension, an integer rather than its image in $F$. Assume $\operatorname{char}F=p>0$. Let $W=N_S(T)(F)/T(F)$ act on $X$ by $(w\chi)(t)=\chi(n_w^{-1}tn_w)$ for a normalizer representative, let $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$, and put $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbf Z\alpha$. Write $\mu<\eta$ if $\eta-\mu$ is a nonzero integral nonnegative combination of simple roots. A character is dominant if its pairing with every simple coroot is nonnegative. For any dominant $\eta\in X$, extend $w_0\eta$ to $\widetilde{w_0\eta}:B\to\mathbf G_m$ through the projection $B\to T$, and define the actual regular-function module
$$I(\eta)=\{f\in F[S]: f(gb)=\widetilde{w_0\eta}(b)^{-1}f(g)\text{ after every commutative }F\text{-algebra extension}\},\qquad (sf)(g)=f(s^{-1}g).$$
It is nonzero finite-dimensional and admits a finite composition series, meaning a strictly increasing finite filtration by rational submodules from zero to $I(\eta)$ with nonzero simple successive quotients. In every such series exactly one quotient has highest weight $\eta$. Every other quotient has a dominant highest weight $\mu<\eta$ and satisfies
$$\mu+\rho=w(\eta+\rho)+p\gamma\quad\text{for some }w\in W,\ \gamma\in Q.$$
This assertion has no restriction on the positive prime characteristic and includes reducible and empty root systems.

source.place: Part II, Chapter 2 (highest-weight structure of induced modules) and Chapter 6 (linkage principle); book WANTED, not local. Corroboration read online: Andersen, The Steinberg linkage class for a reductive algebraic group, arXiv:1706.00590v2, sections 2.2 and 2.8, printed pp.2 and 5; Williamson, Algebraic representations and constructible sheaves, arXiv:1610.06261v1, sections 1.2 and 1.9, pp.4--5 and 12. Our positive Borel convention is implemented by E_B(w_0 eta). Milne 22.21--22.27 gives the actual regular-function convention. No Steinberg simplicity or tensor product theorem is included.

proof.text: Put $\chi=w_0\eta$ and $\lambda=-w_0\eta$. The longest-element statement [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit] gives $w_0^2=1$. Since $-w_0$ carries the positive roots onto themselves, it permutes their indecomposable elements, the simple roots, and their corresponding coroots. Thus $\lambda$ is dominant: its simple-coroot pairings are the simple-coroot pairings of $\eta$ in a permuted order. Here roots, coroots and their pairing are those of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. The regular-function space in the item is literally $I(\eta)=E_B(-\widetilde\lambda)$, with the same left translation. The finite-dimensionality assertion of [lem-sfb-induced-weyl-dimension-formula] applies. For nonvanishing, [lem-sfb-dominant-character-highest-line] supplies a finite-dimensional rational module $V$ and a nonzero $B$-eigenvector $v$ of character $\widetilde\lambda$. Choose an $F$-linear functional $\ell$ with $\ell(v)=1$. The matrix coefficient $f(g)=\ell(gv)$ is regular, satisfies $f(gb)=\widetilde\lambda(b)f(g)$ over every $F$-algebra, and has $f(1)=1$. Hence $I(\eta)\ne0$.

source.place: Definition 22.21, Proposition 22.27(a), pp.468--470; nonvanishing by the matrix-coefficient construction; dimension formula only used for finiteness.

proof.text:
Finite-dimensional rational modules have finite composition series by induction on their vector-space dimension. A nonzero module has a rational submodule of least positive dimension, which is simple. Its quotient has smaller dimension; lift an inductively chosen composition series of the quotient and prepend this simple submodule. The zero-dimensional case has the empty series. We will also use exactness of torus weight spaces, directly from the split-torus coaction: identify $F[T]$ with a Laurent polynomial algebra and write $c(v)=\sum_
u v_
u\otimes z^
u$. Coassociativity and the counit say that $v=\sum_
u v_
u$ is the unique decomposition into weight vectors. An equivariant map preserves these coefficients. In a surjection, extract the $
u$-component of any lift of a $
u$-weight vector; this proves surjectivity on that weight space. Consequently weight dimensions add in every short exact sequence of rational modules.

source.place: Finite-dimensional linear algebra and coefficient extraction in the split-torus coaction; compare section 12 on diagonalizable groups.

proof.text: Write $D=I(\eta)^\vee$ with $(g\ell)(f)=\ell(g^{-1}f)$. The inverse-transpose of the regular action matrix gives its rational coaction. Put $e(f)=f(1)$. The matrix coefficient constructed in step 1 has $e(f)=1$, so $e\ne0$. For $b\in B(A)$, $(be)(f)=f(b)=\widetilde\chi(b)^{-1}f(1)$, so $e$ is a $B$-eigenvector of weight $\lambda=-w_0\eta$. Let $C$ be the smallest rational submodule of $D$ containing $e$. Its annihilator $C^\perp\subseteq I(\eta)$ is rational: the identity $\ell(gf)=(g^{-1}\ell)(f)$ proves stability over every algebra. If $f\in C^\perp$, then $f(g)=(ge)(f)=0$ universally, since $ge\in C\otimes_F A$. Taking $A=F[S]$ and the universal point shows that this is the zero regular function. Thus $C^\perp=0$, and finite-dimensional duality gives $C=D$.

source.place: Definition 22.21 and the evaluation map in 22.29, pp.468 and 470; explicit dual cyclicity by annihilators, without Frobenius reciprocity or a density theorem.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-primitive-cyclic-weight-bound] to the rational module $D$ generated by the $B$-eigenvector $e$ of weight $\lambda$. It gives $\dim_FD_\lambda=1$ and $\lambda-\delta\in\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathbf N\alpha$ for every weight $\delta$ of $D$. For any rational module $M$ and normalizer representative $n_w$, the equality $t(n_wm)=n_w(n_w^{-1}tn_w)m$ gives $M_
u\cong M_{w
u}$. Dualization negates weights, by evaluating the dual action on a weight basis. Hence, for a weight $
u$ of $I(\eta)$, $-w_0
u$ is a weight of $D$, and $w_0(
u-\eta)=\lambda-(-w_0
u)$ is a nonnegative simple-root sum. Apply $-w_0$, which permutes the simple roots as in step 1, to obtain $\eta-
u\in\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathbf N\alpha$. Also $w_0\lambda=-\eta$ by [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit], so $\dim_F I(\eta)_\eta=\dim_FD_{-\eta}=\dim_FD_\lambda=1$.

source.place: Proposition 22.17, p.467, applied to the cyclic dual; Proposition 22.15, p.467, normalizer calculation written explicitly; contragredient weight calculation, p.471.

proof.text: Fix any composition series and a simple quotient $L$ in it. By [lem-sfb-simple-module-dual-highest-weight], $L^U$ is a one-dimensional $T$-eigenline of some weight $\mu$. Because $B=U\rtimes T$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], a nonzero vector $v$ on this line is a $B$-eigenvector of the extension of $\mu$; simplicity says that it generates $L$. The cyclic weight bound [lem-sfb-primitive-cyclic-weight-bound] gives $L_\mu=Fv$ and all weights of $L$ at most $\mu$. The simple roots form a basis of $X\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ by [lem-sfb-simply-connected-character-lattice], so every character lies in the rational root span. For each simple root $\alpha$, the reflection $s_\alpha$ has a normalizer representative by [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization]. Thus $s_\alpha\mu$ is also a weight, by the calculation of step 4, so $\mu-s_\alpha\mu=\langle\mu,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ is a nonnegative simple-root sum. Linear independence of the simple roots makes $\langle\mu,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0$. Thus $\mu$ is dominant. Exactness on weight spaces (step 2) and the weight bound for $I(\eta)$ (step 4) give $\mu\le\eta$.

source.place: Theorem 22.18, pp.467--468; dominance deduced explicitly as in Proposition 22.17 from the weight bound and simple reflections.

proof.text: Take the $\eta$-weight space of every short exact sequence in the chosen series. By step 2 its dimension adds, and the sum of the dimensions of the factors' $\eta$-weight spaces is $\dim_F I(\eta)_\eta=1$. A factor of highest weight $\mu$ can have an $\eta$-weight only if $\eta\le\mu$, by step 5; since also $\mu\le\eta$, the pointed simple-root cone forces $\mu=\eta$. In that case its $\eta$-weight space has dimension one by step 5. Therefore exactly one factor has highest weight $\eta$. All other factors have dominant highest weight $\mu<\eta$. This works for the arbitrary chosen series, with no appeal to a change-of-series theorem.

source.place: Dimension additivity on torus weight spaces and the simple-root partial order; cf. Milne Theorem 22.18 and Proposition 22.27(c).

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-induced-module-primitive-line] applied to $E_B(\widetilde\chi)$, its nonzero $U$-fixed subspace is one-dimensional. The weight there is $w_0\chi=\eta$, using [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit]. Suppose $I(\eta)=A\oplus B'$ for nonzero rational submodules. A least-positive-dimension submodule of $A$, and one of $B'$, are simple. Each has a nonzero $U$-fixed line by [lem-sfb-simple-module-dual-highest-weight]. Their inclusions give two independent $U$-fixed vectors in $I(\eta)$, a contradiction. Consequently $I(\eta)$ is indecomposable as a rational module.

source.place: Proposition 22.22 and Theorem 22.18, pp.467--469; indecomposability follows from the primitive line, not from simplicity of the induced module.

proof.text: To prove linkage use the opposite Borel $B^-=nB n^{-1}$, with $n$ representing $w_0$. Write $H^i(x)=H^i(S/B^-,\mathcal L(F_x))$ in the notation of [lem-sfb-flag-cohomology-finite-exact]. Its degree-zero identification gives an explicit isomorphism $H^0(\eta)\to I(\eta)$: $f\mapsto(g\mapsto f(gn))$. Indeed $bn=n(n^{-1}bn)$, and the $B^-$-character $\eta(n^{-1}bn)$ is the $B$-character $w_0\eta(b)$. Right translation by $n^{-1}$ is the inverse, and both maps commute with left translation. This changes no weights or group action. In what follows, simple constituents have highest weights as in [lem-sfb-simple-module-dual-highest-weight].

source.place: p.55, homogeneous bundles and H^0 convention; explicit change of Borel by right translation.

proof.text: We prove the stronger simultaneous claim $P(x)$ for every $x\in D=\{x:x+\rho\text{ is dominant}\}$: every simple constituent of every $H^i(w\mathbin\cdot x)$, $w\in W$, $i\ge0$, has highest weight $\nu\uparrow x$. Use the well-founded strict order on $D$ and the unique dot-dominant representative from [lem-sfb-affine-reflection-dominant-descent]. Assume $P(y)$ for all $y<x$. Within this outer induction we will induct on $\ell(w)$. The rank-one computation [lem-sfb-minimal-parabolic-line-cohomology] includes the zero fibre at pairing $-1$ and the acyclicity of a $P_\alpha$-module tensored with $F_{-\rho}$, since $\langle-\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=-1$. The reflection sequences [lem-sfb-demazure-reflection-sequences] apply also at $\langle y+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$; there is no omitted wall or small-prime case.

source.place: pp.56--57, Lemma 3, Corollary 2, and outer induction in the proof of Theorem 1.

proof.text: First isolate the error terms used in both induction branches. Let $y=w\mathbin\cdot x$ and $\ell(s_\alpha w)=\ell(w)+1$. The error modules $C,Q'$ in [lem-sfb-demazure-reflection-sequences] have only weights $z=s_\alpha\mathbin\cdot y+kp\alpha$ with $0<kp<\langle y+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle$. By [lem-sfb-flag-cohomology-finite-exact], a constituent of any $H^j(C)$ or $H^j(Q')$ occurs in $H^j(z)$ for one such weight. By [lem-sfb-affine-reflection-dominant-descent], $z=v\mathbin\cdot d(z)$, $d(z)<x$, and $d(z)\uparrow x$. Apply the already available outer hypothesis $P(d(z))$ to get $\nu\uparrow d(z)$. Concatenate its chain with $d(z)\uparrow x$ to obtain $\nu\uparrow x$. The second exact segment in the reflection node makes $H^{i+1}(E)$ an extension of subquotients of $H^{i+1}(C)$ and $H^i(Q')$; hence all its constituents satisfy this conclusion, too. If the error-weight range is empty, those modules are zero. This uses outer induction only, before any assertion at $x$ has been proved.

source.place: p.57, alternatives b), b-prime and b-double-prime; p.58, Lemma 5. Error-term argument written separately to make both inductions noncircular.

proof.text: For the inner base $w=1$, choose simple reflections along a reduced path $w_j=s_{\beta_j}w_{j-1}$, $w_0'=1$, $w_N=w_0$, $\ell(w_j)=j$, and put $x_j=w_j\mathbin\cdot x$. The first reflection segment gives maps $H^{i+j}(x_j)\to H^{i+j-1}(x_{j-1})$ whose cokernels are subquotients of the error cohomology just treated. Iterating, the quotient of $H^i(x)$ by the image of the composite $H^{i+N}(w_0\mathbin\cdot x)\to H^i(x)$ has only constituents $\nu\uparrow x$: for two composable maps the cokernel of their composite is an extension of the second cokernel by a quotient of the first, and induction repeats this. When $i>0$ the source is zero by the dimension-vanishing assertion [lem-sfb-flag-cohomology-finite-exact]. When $i=0$ and $x$ is not dominant, $H^0(x)=0$ by [lem-sfb-top-bottom-cohomology-simple-image]. When $i=0$ and $x$ is dominant, that same node says that the composite has image either zero or $L(x)$; that constituent has weight $x\uparrow x$ (the empty chain). Thus $P(x)$ holds for $w=1$ in every degree, including an outer-minimal $x$ for which no smaller error representative exists.

source.place: pp.57--58, reduced-word composite, dimension cutoff, and Lemma 4. The composite is not assumed nonzero.

proof.text:
For the inner step take $\ell(w)>0$, choose a left descent $\alpha$ and put $v=s_\alpha w$, so $\ell(v)=\ell(w)-1$ and $y=v\mathbin\cdot x$. The first long exact sequence of [lem-sfb-demazure-reflection-sequences] contains
$$H^{i-1}(E)\longrightarrow H^i(w\mathbin\cdot x)\longrightarrow H^{i-1}(v\mathbin\cdot x).$$
The left term's constituents satisfy $\nu\uparrow x$ by the outer-induction error argument, and the right term's by the inner hypothesis. Kernel/image exactness gives the claim for the middle term. In degree zero the negative cohomology terms are zero by convention. This completes both inductions. Applying $P(\eta)$ at $w=1,i=0$ and the explicit isomorphism of step 8 proves strong linkage for each factor of $I(\eta)$.

source.place: p.58, final paragraph of the proof of Theorem 1; shorter left-descent formulation of the same length induction.

proof.text: A step in the chain $\nu\uparrow\eta$ has the form $z'=s_\beta(z+\rho)-\rho+np\beta$. Thus it is a transformation $z\mapsto w(z+\rho)-\rho+p\gamma$ with $\gamma\in Q$. Such transformations are closed under composition: the product of $(w,\gamma)$ and $(v,\delta)$ is $(wv,\gamma+w\delta)$, and $WQ=Q$. A finite chain therefore gives $\nu+\rho=w(\eta+\rho)+p\gamma$ for some $w\in W$, $\gamma\in Q$, exactly as required. Steps 5--6 already give dominance, strict decrease for the other factors and multiplicity one in every composition series. The argument used every positive prime, and the root-system input includes products and rank zero. In rank zero there is no lower factor by step 6, so linkage has no extra case.

source.place: Definition 1, p.54; direct multiplication of affine-root transformations.

Step 9 states P(x) and sets up an outer induction on the well-founded (D,<) and an inner induction on ℓ(w).
